newsitem.title: UK: RUGBY UNION-WELSH SUPREMO CALLS FOR NORTHERN UNITY.
newsitem.headline: RUGBY UNION-WELSH SUPREMO CALLS FOR NORTHERN UNITY.

text.p: Welsh rugby union director Terry Cobner called on Monday for unity among Europe's Five Nations in an attempt to combat the southern hemisphere stranglehold on world rugby.
"We need to go forward together. It should be a case of doing what is best for the northern hemisphere as a whole and not individual countries. We need to get the structure right," he said.
Cobner's comments came after a weekend of international action dominated by southern super powers New Zealand, South Africa and Australia.

The All Blacks, disguised as a star-studded Barbarians side, beat England 34-19 at Twickenham, the world champion Springboks toppled France in Bordeaux while Australia made it six successive wins in a row over Wales on Sunday.
The overall picture since rugby's inaugural World Cup nine years ago makes even bleaker reading.

Wales and Ireland have not beaten any of that illustrious trio, Scotland can boast only two wins from 16 starts and England's record is less than a 50% winning return, although they did triumph against all three during a memorable 19-month spell between November 1993 and June 1995.
In all, British victories number just seven from the last 51 fixtures.
Cobner, a former Wales captain, believes an expanded European Cup competition next season along similar lines to the south's Super 12 series could be a start.
"Two autumn Tests against quality touring opposition would also be slotted in, building up nicely to the Five Nations Championship and then more domestic fixtures towards the end of the season.

"The Five Nations owe it to each other to work much closer together. Collectively, we could improve considerably by agreeing an extended European Cup and seeking far greater exposure to southern hemisphere sides generally."
Kiwi superstar Jonah Lomu, one of several star names who joined Cobner for Monday's coaching clinic in Cardiff, believes British rugby's feuding parties could learn from New Zealand.

"When rugby union went professional back home, it totally drowned out rugby league. Everyone pulled together and learned together. Everything has settled down now and the structure is good," said Lomu.
"I think that British players have all the skills in the world, but sometimes they don't seem to believe in themselves enough."
